title: About the size of Google Scholar: playing the numbers
extended_summary:
This paper does not match the requested 2025 secondary-school writing study. Instead, it is a 2014 working paper about estimating the size of Google Scholar. The authors address the methodological problem of determining how many documents Google Scholar indexes, noting that unlike traditional bibliographic databases, Google Scholar does not transparently report its coverage and its search-result counts are often unstable or inconsistent.

The paper studies four estimation approaches rather than an educational intervention: (1) adapting Khabsa and Giles’s capture-recapture method based on overlap between Google Scholar and Microsoft Academic Search, (2) deriving an estimate from prior empirical comparison studies between Google Scholar and Web of Science, (3) issuing direct queries to Google Scholar year by year, and (4) using so-called absurd queries designed to force Google Scholar to return near-total counts. The context is bibliometric/database analysis, not classrooms, schools, or learners.

No student, teacher, or school population is studied. The authors analyze database behavior and reported hit counts, drawing on search interfaces for Google Scholar, Microsoft Academic Search, and Web of Science. They also discuss database biases by language and document type, as well as technical problems such as duplicate records, faulty hit count estimates, and inconsistencies in date-range querying.

The main conclusion is that all available estimation methods have serious limitations, but they converge loosely on a broad estimate of roughly 160 million Google Scholar records as of May 2014. The authors argue that Google Scholar’s opacity makes rigorous estimation unnecessarily difficult and that Google itself could provide a definitive figure. Because this is not an AI-in-education or writing-intervention study, the requested details about secondary students, writing outcomes, generative AI use, rubrics, and treatment effects are not present in the supplied text.
quality_tier_rationale: The provided document is a 2014 working paper about estimating the size of Google Scholar, not a study of an educational AI intervention. It does not evaluate student writing, secondary-school learners, or any writing-feedback technology, and the text provided is grey literature rather than a peer-reviewed intervention study.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention impact on student outcomes is studied in this paper. Therefore there is no evidence of impact on secondary students' writing or any other educational outcome.
